databaselibraryreadingslab

“We propose that artistic practice be viewed as the production of knowledge or philosophy in action.”

Estelle Barrett and Barbara Bolt (eds), Practice as Research: Approaches to Creative Arts Enquiry; Owen Chapman and Kim Sawchuk, “Research-Creation: Intervention, Analysis and ‘Family Resemblances’”

a third species of research

  • “Practice-led researchers are formulating a third species of research, one that stands in alignment with, but separate to, the established quantitative and qualitative research traditions.” 150
  • “We demonstrate further, that practice-led research is a new species of research, generative enquiry that draws on subjective, interdisciplinary and emergent methodologies that have the potential to extend the frontiers of research.” 1
  • “What new knowledge/understandings did the studio enquiry and methodology generate that may not have been revealed through other research approaches?” 1

practice is primary, and it is not illustration

  • “Practice is primary; it should never illustrate theory. It is easy to lose track of this when conducting the literature review.” 190
  • “Above all, it asserts the primacy of practice and insists that because creative practice is both ongoing and persistent; practitioner researchers do not merely 'think' their way through or out of a problem, but rather they 'practise' to a resolution.” 147
  • “It is my contention that it is art as a mode of revealing and as a material productivity, not just the artwork that constitutes creative arts research.” 34

material thinking

  • “Rather, we come to know the world theoretically only after we have come to understand it through handling.” 30
  • “Material thinking is the logic of practice.” 30
  • “In this conception, the materials are not just passive objects to be used instrumentally by the artist, but rather, the materials and processes of production have their own intelligence that come into play in interaction with the artist's creative intelligence.” 29
  • “The materials and methods used in the studio form part of the enquiry itself—often the process involves inventing new methods and using new or unconventional materials.” 191

the method emerges with the work

  • “As a result of this reflexive process, methodologies in artistic research are necessarily emergent and subject to repeated adjustment, rather than remaining fixed throughout the process of enquiry.” 6
  • “However, we can not consciously seek the new, since by definition the new can not be known in advance.” 31
  • “Thus the new can be seen to emerge in the involvement with materials, methods, tools and ideas of practice.” 30
  • “The 'shock of the new' is thus a particular understanding that is realised through our dealings with the tools and materials of production and in our handling of ideas, rather than a selfconscious attempt at transgression.” 31

the writing: the exegesis

  • “In other words, through the vehicle of the exegesis, practice becomes theory generating.” 33
  • “The task of the exegesis is not just to explain or contextualise practice, but rather is to produce movement in thought itself.” 33
  • “It is also crucial to write about the studio production and outcomes as research. The exegesis is primarily concerned with process rather than product.” 202
  • “The significance of the work should focus on the question: What has the studio enquiry revealed that could not have been revealed through other modes of research?” 199

the shape of the enquiry, and of the writing

  • “The abstract is a ‘mini’ exegesis – it summarises the following: Aim; Methods/content; New understandings/outcomes; Significance and relevance of the enquiry.” 201

the case studies

3 · Perry — the novel and its exegesis“A considerable part of my discussion centered on the suggestion that creative work could be recognised as valid research within itself, without necessarily requiring exegesis.” 35
4 · Reid — the camera in the rehearsal“In choreographing for video, I am exploring mechanisms by which I can translate the kinaesthetic intimacy of dance and the body to the screen—to make my sweat bead on the surface of the screen.” 47
5 · Iggulden — words and images in the studio“by drawing on the generative aspects of silence to work with words and images within the studio, I found an alternative avenue for my voice and the means to articulate my experience of silence” 65
6 · McLeod — structured improvisation“The outcome is a dual record, danced and written, of an investigation into how dance might express and reveal masculine subjectivity.” 82
7 · Vincs — the dance–writing machine“The dance and the writing had to function with one another one the same epistemological level, as a dance–writing machine rather than adopting a hierarchical structure in which one precedes and the other explains.” 105
8 · Goddard — the video postcard“An exegesis can neither exist as the final word, nor an end to meanings.” 119
9 · Stewart — bricolage and the neonarrative“My argument linking artist/researcher/teacher centres on the notion that if we, as practitioners, can understand and situate our practice, then we own the practice.” 132

the term, and what it intervenes into

  • “In Britain and Australia, this is typically framed as “practice as research” (see, for example, Barrett and Bolt, 2010), whereas in the U.S., it is called “arts-based research” (see, for example, Leavy, 2009) and/or rolled into discussions regarding “creative arts PhDs” (Elkins, 2009).” 6
  • “Research-creation is not so much a “new” method as it is a “newly recognized” academic practice that has gained ground in the past ten years.” 6
  • “the focus of this article is how this practice acts as an epistemological intervention into the “regime of truth” of the university (Foucault, 1980)” 6
  • “Research-creation can thus be read as a methodological and epistemological challenge to the argumentative form(s) that have typified much academic scholarship.” 6

the four modes, held by family resemblance

  • “Knowledge is produced as creative work, and not simply through their analysis and interpretation.” 21
  • “Creative productions constitute knowledge in a different, but culturally equivalent, way to other forms of transcribed research findings, such as academic journal articles, scholarly books, mathematical formulae, research reports, studies, theses, et cetera.” 21
  • “Clearly, these categories are not easily separated, and each is connected to the others. Further, they do not merely occur in a linear sequence, but can be ongoing, and happen simultaneously.” 21
  • “I want what counts as “theory” and what counts as “practice” to be rendered bankrupt at binary oppositions, but not through unity, though a situated complexity.” 20

what an institution does with the term

  • “What is important from the Council’s definition is that research is situated as a part of an investigation that involves trying things out, as opposed to a gathering data, as it is often conceived in traditional academia.” 9
  • “These definitions seem intent to set up criteria adopted from conventional research assessment methods for application to research-creation. The specific uniqueness of research-creation is not defined” 9
  • “new bureaucratic exercises, such as the imposition of “metrics” to measure and evaluate academic research across disciplines, threaten to introduce mechanisms that will impose new forms of standardization” 7
  • “Research-creation projects must be assessed with a rigorous flexibility, and without resorting solely to putatively objective evaluation criteria.” 22
  • “Reviewers must be selected who can recognize the terrains upon which a project intervenes, and speak to these considerations in their deliberations.” 23

where the two texts meet, and where they part

  • “Barrett and Bolt (2010), Leavy (2009), and Haseman (2006) all underscore that positivist, quantitative research is often defaulted to as the easiest to support in terms of grants and other forms of established acknowledgment of a research program’s potential.” 11
  • “Both Leavy (2009) and Barrett and Bolt (2010) view research-creation as a form of intervention because it is contradictory to a hierarchy of research significance that places the scientific method at the pinnacle of models for knowledge production and dissemination.” 11
  • “Our emphasis on research-creation’s ability to challenge academic standards and criteria markers is distinct from Leavy (2009), Barrett and Bolt (2010) and Haseman’s (2006) attempts to advance the field within the folds of academic legitimacy.” 13
  • “Suggesting that research-creation can pass through credibility tests stemming from sanctioned metrics for qualitative research programs reads as a form of apologetics.” 13
